The number of individuals who report injecting drugs within the past 1, 3, 6, or 12 months may be relatively small compared to the overall sample size, depending on the nature of the population being studied. For more details on collecting data from behavioral surveys, refer to page 17. 2. When setting targets, the results of an initial survey can serve as a baseline for this indicator. Countries can then establish a target and a timeline for achieving it. 3. For NSP (Needle and Syringe Program) coverage, baseline levels should first be measured. Countries should set ambitious yet realistic targets and timelines to scale up NSPs, aiming to increase reach both in absolute terms (e.g., NSP-4a, NSP-4c, NSP-4e) and relative to the estimated size of key populations (e.g., NSP-4b, NSP-4d, NSP-4f). 4. Indicative targets for NSP-3d (percentage of people who inject drugs accessing an NSP at least once per month over 12 months) can be used as benchmarks. Possible target levels include low (20%), mid (60%), and high. The high target is based on retrospective analysis of coverage in urban settings in high-income countries. 5. Target levels for NSP-4b should be set higher, as this indicator measures access at any point during the reporting period rather than regular reach. Similarly, targets for NSP-4f should also be higher, as this indicator may include double counting of individuals accessing services multiple times. 6. National guidelines for NSPs should ensure there is no limit on the quantity of injecting equipment provided, and the return of used equipment should not be a prerequisite for receiving new supplies. However, individuals should be encouraged and supported to safely dispose of used equipment. 7. NSPs should provide a range of injecting equipment appropriate for local practices and substances, ensuring acceptability to the target population. People who inject drugs should be consulted to determine the most suitable equipment for distribution. Ideally, the smallest gauge needles should be provided to minimize tissue damage, while larger gauge needles may be necessary for certain drugs, such as those with higher viscosity. 8. Syringes should be of appropriate volume, with larger syringes available for substances injected in greater volumes, such as methadone. Materials to encourage non-injecting routes of administration, such as sterile pipes, papers, or foil, should also be provided as safer alternatives to injecting. 9. When conducting audits of current legislation and policies, the checklist items can help identify laws and policies that may support or negatively impact the rights, health, or welfare of key populations, including people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, people in prisons, sex workers, and transgender individuals. Where reforms are needed, processes for change should be identified and evaluated. 10. For opioid substitution therapy (OST), the number of sites providing maintenance OST should be documented. These sites may include specialist services, general practitioners, pharmacies, and mobile dispensing services. The availability of OST is a critical indicator for monitoring program scale-up. 11. OST services should be accessible to key populations, including men who have sex with men, people in prisons, sex workers, and transgender individuals, without fear of stigma or discrimination. Ideally, all mainstream services should meet key population sensitization standards. 12. Countries should aim for OST capacity to meet demand, minimizing the number of people on waiting lists and the duration of waiting times. Targets and timelines should be based on logistical assessments and resource requirements for scaling up OST. 13. OST coverage indicators should ensure that numerators and denominators match. For example, if the numerator is the total number of individuals on OST, the denominator should include all opioid-dependent individuals, regardless of whether they inject drugs. 14. National OST guidelines should be evidence-based, reflect local laws and conditions, and align with international guidance. They should include clear protocols for patient assessment, informed consent, dosing, psychosocial support, dispensing, follow-up, and OST provision for pregnant women. 15. OST prescribers should receive accredited training, participate in continuing education, and be registered to prescribe OST. They should demonstrate respect and non-judgmental attitudes toward people who inject drugs. 16. OST should be affordable to maximize access. This may involve offering OST free of charge, covering costs through health insurance, or subsidizing costs for financially disadvantaged patients. 17. OST retention for at least six months is a critical indicator, as evidence shows that maximum benefit is achieved with treatment lasting at least this duration. Baseline levels should be measured, and countries should set ambitious but realistic targets to maximize retention rates. 18. OST programs should aim to provide maintenance doses that meet or exceed the recommended minimum (e.g., ≥60 mg methadone or ≥12 mg buprenorphine). Baseline levels should be measured, and targets should aim to maximize the percentage of patients receiving adequate maintenance doses. 19. Psychosocial support is an essential component of OST. The percentage of OST patients receiving psychosocial support within the past 12 months should be monitored, with targets set to ensure comprehensive care.
